splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year, or whether actuaries may adopt assumptions after that date. The outcome affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers participating in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be selected by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that actuaries may select assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing use of more current data in calculations.

circuits.name: D.C. Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year and raises questions about judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release terms are tolled during periods of absconding, so the clock stops running when a supervisee flees.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release terms when a supervisee absconds, and courts lack authority to create such a doctrine.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: There is a longstanding 6-to-3 circuit split on whether federal prisoners face a categorical bar under § 2244(b)(1) from raising any claim they previously presented in a successive § 2255 motion, in addition to the separate requirements in § 2255(h). The outcome determines whether federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement than Congress intended for successive collateral attacks.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, categorically barring any claim they previously presented.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, meaning they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on what a candidate must show to establish standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The outcome could reshape how courts evaluate candidate standing for election-related lawsuits, affecting rules on mail-in voting, ballot counting deadlines, and election administration nationwide.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have Article III standing to challenge election rules that allegedly dilute lawful votes or alter election procedures, even before the election takes place.

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates cannot establish concrete injury sufficient for standing merely from the existence of a ballot-counting rule, as the alleged harm is too speculative or generalized.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency or Sentencing Commission deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous provisions in criminal sentencing guidelines.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether lenity trumps deference to agency interpretations in criminal or sentencing contexts. At least three circuits hold that lenity prevails over deference, while others (including the Third Circuit panel) have held that agency deference can trump lenity. The issue is of heightened importance after Loper Bright overruled Chevron.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes priority over Auer/Kisor or Chevron deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal or sentencing provisions, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability through delegated interpretive power.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference can take precedence over the rule of lenity when the agency has authoritatively interpreted an ambiguous guideline or regulation in the criminal context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether 'and' in § 3553(f)(1) means a defendant is disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria or if meeting any single criterion suffices. This split leads to dramatically different sentencing outcomes for defendants with identical criminal histories depending on their circuit of conviction.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as 'or' based on context and statutory structure.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' commentary (Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2) can authoritatively expand the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, when the guideline text does not mention them.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether Application Note 1's inclusion of conspiracy and other inchoate offenses in the definition of 'controlled substance offense' is entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor, or whether the guideline text unambiguously excludes such offenses. This split affects career-offender designations that dramatically increase sentences.

positions.label: Commentary is authoritative — inchoate offenses included
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is entitled to deference as an authoritative interpretation of the ambiguous guideline, and inchoate offenses like conspiracy qualify as controlled substance offenses for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Guideline text controls — inchoate offenses excluded
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously does not include inchoate offenses, and Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the definition beyond its textual scope, so it is not entitled to deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) when the state schedule criminalizes substances not controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the career-offender guideline's 'controlled substance offense' definition requires the underlying substance to be controlled under federal law, or whether any state-controlled substance suffices. This affects career-offender determinations and base offense levels for defendants with prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: State law controls — no federal-law limitation
positions.summary: Holds that § 4B1.2(b) broadly includes 'an offense under state law' and there is no textual basis to graft a federal-law limitation onto the guideline's definition.

positions.label: Federal schedules control
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly impose sentences at supervised release revocation proceedings for the purpose of punishing the defendant for the violation, or whether revocation sentences must be limited to promoting the goals of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether supervised release revocation can serve a punitive purpose. The Sixth Circuit (under United States v. Lewis) permits express punishment at revocation, placing it at the extreme of a circuit split, while other circuits hold that revocation sentences must focus on the purposes of supervised release rather than punishment for the violation.

positions.label: Punishment is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release at revocation proceedings, not limited to deterrence or rehabilitation goals.

positions.label: Punishment is not a proper purpose
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences should be tailored to the goals of supervised release and that expressly punishing the defendant for the violation is impermissible.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the First Step Act's non-retroactive change to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) stacking can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), and whether the Sentencing Commission's policy statement (U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6)) permitting such consideration exceeds its statutory authority.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether non-retroactive sentencing changes (particularly the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to § 924(c)) can support compassionate release, and whether the Sentencing Commission can override circuit precedent through its policy statements. The Seventh and Eighth Circuits hold that such changes cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons, while other circuits have allowed consideration of these changes.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, whether offered alone or in combination with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' under § 3582(c)(1)(A), and the Sentencing Commission cannot override this by policy statement.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider non-retroactive sentencing changes as part of the totality of circumstances in evaluating extraordinary and compelling reasons, consistent with the Sentencing Commission's policy statement.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging the conditions or terms of their confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) must proceed via habeas corpus or may bring civil rights actions (Bivens or § 1983).
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for federal prisoners challenging conditions that affect the terms of confinement (such as BOP decisions on First Step Act time credits or transfer to prerelease custody), or whether such claims may also be brought as civil rights actions. The Supreme Court has noted but never resolved this question since Preiser v. Rodriguez (1973).

positions.label: Habeas is exclusive for duration/terms challenges
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to BOP decisions affecting the duration or terms of confinement, including First Step Act time credit applications, must be brought exclusively through habeas corpus.

positions.label: Civil rights actions also available for conditions claims
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may bring civil rights actions (under § 1983 or Bivens) to challenge conditions of confinement even when habeas might also be available, as long as they do not challenge the fact or duration of confinement itself.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil appeal deadline (60 days for government-party cases) or the criminal appeal deadline (14 days) applies to appeals from orders on Hyde Amendment motions for attorney's fees in criminal cases.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (triggering the civil appeal deadline) or part of the criminal case itself (triggering the shorter criminal deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies, but acknowledged a lopsided circuit split.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the civil appeal deadline under FRAP 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is part of the criminal case, so the criminal appeal deadline under FRAP 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor when a Chapter 13 case is converted to Chapter 7 in good faith under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 348(f)(1)(A)'s reference to 'property of the estate, as of the date of filing' means the estate captures only the value of the asset at filing or includes post-petition appreciation. The Ninth Circuit held appreciation belongs to the estate, while other circuits have held it belongs to the debtor. This split has significant implications for debtors who convert in good faith after their home values increase.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the broad scope of § 541(a) means that post-petition appreciation in property value inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that § 348(f)(1)(A) was designed to protect good-faith converting debtors, and post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtor, not the estate.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal court filings containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that denials of motions to seal medical information are immediately appealable as collateral orders because medical privacy is a value of 'high order,' while other circuits have not extended the collateral order doctrine to seal denials. This creates tension with the Supreme Court's narrow approach to collateral order jurisdiction in Mohawk Industries.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that an order denying a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because maintaining medical privacy is a value of high order that would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal are not immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine, as the Supreme Court has cautioned against expanding the narrow categories of appealable interlocutory orders.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute or contribute to an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law can be considered as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release. Some circuits hold that non-retroactive changes in law can never contribute to such a finding, while others and the Sentencing Commission's 2024 policy statement (§ 1B1.13(b)(6)) allow consideration of such changes. This affects large numbers of federal prisoners serving sentences under now-repealed mandatory minimums.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether alone or in combination with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for a sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may contribute to compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered as one factor among others in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release, consistent with the Sentencing Commission's 2024 policy statement.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA permits suits for money damages against prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits allow such suits while others hold that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages, raising questions about the scope of Congressional spending power to impose personal liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA allows individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA authorizes suits for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities, as the statute's text is broad enough to encompass such claims.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Landor v. Louisiana Dep't of Corrections

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and Spending Clause legislation cannot impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments under federal civil rights law?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve disagreement among circuits over the standards for discrimination claims against hospitality and business operators, including questions about liability and available remedies. The Second Circuit's approach was deemed sufficiently unsettled to warrant review.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that broader standards apply to discrimination claims against business establishments, potentially allowing for more expansive remedies.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that narrower standards govern such claims, limiting the scope of liability and available remedies for discrimination in public accommodations.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
